subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Conservation of mass and balanced equations

questions.lo: Conservation of mass and balanced equations
questions.q: In a closed system, the total mass of the products of a chemical reaction is always:
options: Equal to the total mass of the reactants
Greater than the total mass of the reactants
Half the total mass of the reactants
Less than the total mass of the reactants
questions.explain: Mass is conserved: no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants in a closed system.

questions.lo: Conservation of mass and balanced equations
questions.q: When magnesium is burned in an open crucible, the mass appears to increase. Why?
options: Magnesium atoms get heavier when heated
A gas is given off during the reaction
Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium to form magnesium oxide
The crucible loses mass to the magnesium
questions.explain: The mass rises because oxygen from the air is added to the solid to form MgO. Mass is still conserved overall if the gas is included.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate, CaCO3? (Ar: Ca=40, C=12, O=16)
What is the Mr of ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4? (Ar: N=14, H=1, S=32, O=16)
The Avogadro constant is the number of particles in one mole. Its value is approximately:
questions.explain: One mole of any substance contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles (atoms, molecules or ions), the Avogadro constant.

questions.q: How many moles are there in 88 g of carbon dioxide, CO2? (Mr of CO2 = 44)
questions.explain: moles = mass / Mr = 88 / 44 = 2 mol.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? (Mr = 40)
questions.explain: mass = moles x Mr = 0.25 x 40 = 10 g.

questions.q: For the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many moles of water are made from 3 mol of hydrogen (with excess oxygen)?
questions.explain: The ratio of H2 to H2O is 2:2, i.e. 1:1, so 3 mol H2 makes 3 mol H2O.

questions.q: 0.6 mol of a metal M reacts with 0.9 mol of oxygen atoms. What is the simplest formula of the oxide?
questions.explain: Ratio M:O = 0.6 : 0.9 = 2 : 3, so the formula is M2O3.

questions.q: In a reaction, the limiting reactant is the one that:
options: Is left over at the end
Has the highest relative formula mass
Is completely used up, limiting the amount of product formed
questions.explain: The limiting reactant is fully used up first, so it determines (limits) how much product can form; the other reactant is in excess.

questions.q: For Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, if 0.1 mol Mg reacts with 0.15 mol HCl, which is the limiting reactant?
questions.explain: 0.1 mol Mg needs 0.2 mol HCl, but only 0.15 mol HCl is present, so HCl runs out first and is limiting.

questions.q: What is the concentration in g/dm3 of a solution containing 20 g of solute in 250 cm3?
questions.explain: 250 cm3 = 0.25 dm3. Concentration = 20 / 0.25 = 80 g/dm3.

questions.q: What is the concentration in mol/dm3 of a solution with 0.5 mol dissolved in 2 dm3?
questions.explain: Concentration = moles / volume = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol/dm3.

questions.q: Percentage yield is calculated as:
options: (mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100
(moles of product / moles of reactant) x 100
(mass of reactants / mass of products) x 100
(maximum theoretical mass / mass actually made) x 100
questions.explain: Percentage yield = (actual mass of product / theoretical maximum mass) x 100.

questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 50 g but only 40 g of product is made. What is the percentage yield?
Which of these is NOT a reason a reaction may have a yield below 100%?
options: Mass is destroyed during the reaction
There are unexpected side reactions producing other products
Some product is lost when separated or purified
The reaction is reversible and does not go to completion
questions.explain: Mass is never destroyed. Lower yields come from reversible reactions, losses on handling, or competing side reactions.

questions.q: Atom economy is calculated as:
options: (mass of waste / mass of product) x 100
(Mr of reactants / Mr of desired product) x 100
(Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100
questions.explain: Atom economy = (relative formula mass of desired product / sum of relative formula masses of all reactants) x 100.

questions.q: Why is high atom economy important for sustainable manufacturing?
options: It always increases the reaction rate
It reduces waste products and makes better use of raw materials
questions.explain: A high atom economy means more of the reactant atoms end up in the useful product, reducing waste and conserving resources.

questions.q: At room temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3. What volume does 0.5 mol of CO2 occupy?
questions.explain: Volume = moles x 24 = 0.5 x 24 = 12 dm3 at rtp.

questions.q: 25 cm3 of NaOH is neutralised by 20 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl (1:1 ratio). What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explain: Moles HCl = 0.020 x 0.1 = 0.002 mol = moles NaOH. Concentration NaOH = 0.002 / 0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm3.
